newsitem.title: USA: Ethics panel struggles with last act on Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Ethics panel struggles with last act on Gingrich.

text.p: A sharply divided House of Representatives Ethics Committee struggled on Wednesday to clear the way for the final phase of its investigation of Speaker Newt Gingrich and meet a Jan. 21 deadline.
"It's all about process and schedule," the committee's top Democrat, Rep Jim McDermott of Washington, said during a break in the closed-door talks.

A subcommittee that investigated charges against Gingrich for two years said it needed more time to complete the final phase in which the full committee has to decide what penalty to recommend to the full House.
This process will involve hearings in which the ethics committee's findings against Gingrich will be laid out in a public arena for the first time.
But the Republican-controlled House, acting some three hours after Gingrich was narrowly re-elected speaker Tuesday, blocked any extension.

McDermott, speaking to reporters after nearly seven hours of talks, said the committee had been having a wide range of discussions, including on such questions as: "How many witnesses? How long? When does it start? Which room?"
Committee Chairwoman Nancy Johnson, R-Connecticut, said earlier: "We're working together, and we're doing well."
The Jan. 21 date was agreed on by the committee last month but investigators said on Tuesday they needed more time to ensure a "fair and orderly" process.

Democrats sought on Tuesday to eliminate a provision in the House rules that would put the current ethics committee out of business after Jan. 21, but they were blocked by the House in a virtual party line vote that split the committee. But the two Republicans on the four-member Gingrich subcommittee backed the Democrats' call for more time.

Gingrich admitted on Dec. 21 he had failed to get legal advice to ensure compliance with a ban on using tax-exempt funds for partisan political activity and had given false information to investigators, which he has said was unintentional.
The call for extra time for the last phase of the investigation was spelled out in a statement on Tuesday by James Cole, a special counsel leading the probe.

"In analysing the time necessary for a sanctions hearing and a vote on the House floor, I have recommended a schedule that will allow this to be accomplished in a fair and orderly fashion," he said. "In doing that, however, it will be necessary for the vote on the House floor to occur after Jan. 21, 1977."

Cole said the subcommittee agreed with this view. But full ethics committee member David Hobson, an Ohio Republican, told the House the Democratic motion, which contained no end-date, meant the affair could "go on forever and ever."
McDermott told the House Gingrich's attorney called Cole on Monday to say he would not be ready for hearings until Jan. 13 and needed time to prepare.

"We are being forced into a schedule which is being designed for political damage control," McDermott said, charging Republicans wanted to have the House vote on Jan. 20 -- presidential inauguration day.
